questions.q: The correct decreasing order of basicity is:
questions.explain: The ortho methyls twist the bulky –NMe₂ group out of plane (SIR), localising its lone pair, while with the small –NH₂ group they mainly crowd the –NH₃⁺ ion (ortho effect) and lower basicity.

questions.q: Which compound is the more acidic of the pair, and why? 2,6-dimethyl-4-nitrophenol (P) or 3,5-dimethyl-4-nitrophenol (Q).
options: Q, because methyl groups beside NO₂ increase its −M effect
P, because in Q the methyls twist the NO₂ group out of plane and its −M effect is lost
Q, because methyl groups beside OH destabilise the phenoxide ion in P
Both are equally acidic because the methyl groups have the same +I effect
questions.explain: In Q the methyl groups flank the nitro group and force it out of the ring plane, so it can no longer delocalise the phenoxide charge. In P the nitro group stays coplanar and acidity is similar to p-nitrophenol.

questions.q: In which compound does the SIR effect NOT significantly change the property compared with the parent compound without ortho methyl groups?
questions.explain: A cyano group is linear, so flanking methyl groups cannot twist it out of plane and the acidity changes very little. In the other three, an ortho group twists a resonance-active group and changes the property.

questions.q: o-Toluic acid (pKa 3.9) is stronger than benzoic acid (pKa 4.2). The steric inhibition of resonance explanation is:
options: The ortho methyl group increases conjugation of COOH with the ring, stabilising the anion
The ortho methyl group twists COOH out of the ring plane, removing ring–C=O conjugation that stabilises the undissociated acid
The methyl group withdraws electrons by −I effect from the carboxyl group
The methyl group hydrogen-bonds to the carboxylate oxygen
questions.explain: Ring–C=O conjugation normally stabilises the un-ionised acid; twisting COOH out of plane removes this, so the acid ionises more easily. Note that SIR here raises acidity, unlike the nitrophenol case where it lowers it.
